claim: Dravet syndrome (DS) is a form of epilepsy with a high incidence of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).
source: Dravet syndrome (DS) is a form of epilepsy with a high incidence of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of Dravet syndrome in the medical literature.

claim: Respiratory failure is a leading cause of SUDEP.
source: Respiratory failure is a leading cause of SUDEP
evidence: This statement is supported by established medical knowledge about SUDEP mechanisms.

claim: DS patients frequently exhibit disordered breathing.
source: DS patients' frequently exhibit disordered breathing.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about DS patients referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanisms underlying respiratory dysfunction in DS are unknown.
source: Despite this, mechanisms underlying respiratory dysfunction in DS are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Mice expressing a DS-associated Scn1a missense mutation (A1783V) conditionally in inhibitory neurons exhibit spontaneous seizures.
source: We found that mice expressing a DS-associated Scn1a missense mutation (A1783V) conditionally in inhibitory neurons (Slc32a1cre/+::Scn1aA1783V fl/+; defined as Scn1aΔE26) exhibit spontaneous seizures
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data including ECoG recordings and behavioral observations.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice die prematurely.
source: We found that mice expressing a DS-associated Scn1a missense mutation (A1783V) conditionally in inhibitory neurons (Slc32a1cre/+::Scn1aA1783V fl/+; defined as Scn1aΔE26) exhibit spontaneous seizures, die prematurely
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data showing 100% lethality by 25 days postnatal.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice present a respiratory phenotype including hypoventilation.
source: We found that mice expressing a DS-associated Scn1a missense mutation (A1783V) conditionally in inhibitory neurons (Slc32a1cre/+::Scn1aA1783V fl/+; defined as Scn1aΔE26) exhibit spontaneous seizures, die prematurely and present a respiratory phenotype including hypoventilation
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing reduced minute ventilation.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice present a respiratory phenotype including apnea.
source: We found that mice expressing a DS-associated Scn1a missense mutation (A1783V) conditionally in inhibitory neurons (Slc32a1cre/+::Scn1aA1783V fl/+; defined as Scn1aΔE26) exhibit spontaneous seizures, die prematurely and present a respiratory phenotype including hypoventilation, apnea
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing increased apnea duration.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice present a diminished ventilatory response to CO2.
source: We found that mice expressing a DS-associated Scn1a missense mutation (A1783V) conditionally in inhibitory neurons (Slc32a1cre/+::Scn1aA1783V fl/+; defined as Scn1aΔE26) exhibit spontaneous seizures, die prematurely and present a respiratory phenotype including hypoventilation, apnea, and a diminished ventilatory response to CO2.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing reduced minute ventilation response to graded CO2 increases.

claim: Inhibitory neurons expressing the Scn1a A1783V variant in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) are less excitable in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: At the cellular level in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), we found inhibitory neurons expressing the Scn1a A1783V variant are less excitable
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings showing reduced basal activity and diminished firing responses to depolarizing current injections.

claim: Glutamatergic chemosensitive RTN neurons are hyper-excitable in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: whereas glutamatergic chemosensitive RTN neurons, which are a key source of the CO2/H+-dependent drive to breathe, are hyper-excitable in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings showing enhanced basal activity and CO2/H+ sensitivity.

claim: Glutamatergic chemosensitive RTN neurons are a key source of the CO2/H+-dependent drive to breathe.
source: whereas glutamatergic chemosensitive RTN neurons, which are a key source of the CO2/H+-dependent drive to breathe, are hyper-excitable in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RTN neuron function in respiratory control.

claim: Loss of Scn1a function can disrupt respiratory control at the cellular level.
source: These results show loss of Scn1a function can disrupt respiratory control at the cellular and whole animal levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the cellular electrophysiology data showing altered activity of RTN neurons.

claim: Loss of Scn1a function can disrupt respiratory control at the whole animal level.
source: These results show loss of Scn1a function can disrupt respiratory control at the cellular and whole animal levels.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing respiratory dysfunction in Scn1aΔE26 mice.

claim: Most DS cases (70–95%) are caused by mutations in the Scn1a gene.
source: Most DS cases (70–95%) are caused by mutations in the Scn1a gene (MIM#182389), which encodes the pore-forming subunit of a voltage-gated Na+ channel (Nav1.1) (Meisler and Kearney, 2005; Fujiwara, 2006; Catterall et al., 2010; Akiyama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Scn1a gene encodes the pore-forming subunit of a voltage-gated Na+ channel (Nav1.1).
source: Most DS cases (70–95%) are caused by mutations in the Scn1a gene (MIM#182389), which encodes the pore-forming subunit of a voltage-gated Na+ channel (Nav1.1) (Meisler and Kearney, 2005; Fujiwara, 2006; Catterall et al., 2010; Akiyama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established molecular biology knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 700 different Scn1a pathological variants have been identified in DS patients.
source: Approximately 700 different Scn1a pathological variants have been identified in DS patients, the majority of which are missense or frameshift mutations that result in loss of function (Parihar and Ganesh, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The majority of Scn1a pathological variants in DS patients are missense or frameshift mutations that result in loss of function.
source: Approximately 700 different Scn1a pathological variants have been identified in DS patients, the majority of which are missense or frameshift mutations that result in loss of function (Parihar and Ganesh, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Homozygous Scn1a knockout mice develop ataxia and die at 15 days postnatal.
source: For example, homozygous Scn1a knockout mice develop ataxia and die at 15 days postnatal, whereas heterozygous Scn1a deficient mice show seizure activity and early mortality starting at 3 weeks of age (Yu et al., 2006; Ogiwara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heterozygous Scn1a deficient mice show seizure activity and early mortality starting at 3 weeks of age.
source: For example, homozygous Scn1a knockout mice develop ataxia and die at 15 days postnatal, whereas heterozygous Scn1a deficient mice show seizure activity and early mortality starting at 3 weeks of age (Yu et al., 2006; Ogiwara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Global deletion of Scn1a suppresses activity of inhibitory but not excitatory neurons in the cortex and hippocampus.
source: The cellular basis for many features of DS including seizures and premature death appears to involve disinhibition, as global deletion of Scn1a suppresses activity of inhibitory but not excitatory neurons in the cortex and hippocampus (Yu et al., 2006; Dutton et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Conditional deletion of Scn1a from forebrain inhibitory neurons results in a DS-like phenotype similar to global Scn1a deletion.
source: and conditional deletion of Scn1a from forebrain inhibitory neurons results in a DS-like phenotype similar to global Scn1a deletion (Cheah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Scn1a missense mutations represent ~40% of DS-associated mutations.
source: For these reasons, most studies have used global or inhibitory neuron-specific Scn1a deletions to model DS (Catterall, 2012), with few studies focusing on other high-priority genetic risk factors like Scn1a missense mutations, which represent ~40% of DS-associated mutations (Depienne et al., 2009; Parihar and Ganesh, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The A1783V variant is a DS mutation.
source: The A1783V variant is a DS mutation (Marini et al., 2007; Lossin, 2009; Klassen et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies identifying this mutation in DS patients.

claim: The A1783V variant is predicted to result in loss of function by increasing Nav1.1 voltage-dependent inactivation.
source: The A1783V variant is a DS mutation (Marini et al., 2007; Lossin, 2009; Klassen et al., 2014) predicted to result in loss of function by increasing Nav1.1 voltage-dependent inactivation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the location of the mutation and previous functional studies.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice are on a 90% C57BL6/J: : 10% 129/SvJ background.
source: We found that Scn1aΔE26 mice (on a 90% C57BL6/J: : 10% 129/SvJ background) exhibited spontaneous seizure activity and premature death starting at ~2 weeks of age
evidence: This is a description of the genetic background of the experimental animals.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibited spontaneous seizure activity starting at ~2 weeks of age.
source: We found that Scn1aΔE26 mice (on a 90% C57BL6/J: : 10% 129/SvJ background) exhibited spontaneous seizure activity and premature death starting at ~2 weeks of age
evidence: This is supported by ECoG recordings and behavioral observations.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibited premature death starting at ~2 weeks of age.
source: We found that Scn1aΔE26 mice (on a 90% C57BL6/J: : 10% 129/SvJ background) exhibited spontaneous seizure activity and premature death starting at ~2 weeks of age
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data.

claim: At ~2 weeks of age, Scn1aΔE26 mice hypoventilate.
source: At this same developmental time point, Scn1aΔE26 mice hypoventilate, exhibit frequent apneas under baseline conditions, and show a reduced ventilatory response to CO2.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data.

claim: At ~2 weeks of age, Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibit frequent apneas under baseline conditions.
source: At this same developmental time point, Scn1aΔE26 mice hypoventilate, exhibit frequent apneas under baseline conditions, and show a reduced ventilatory response to CO2.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing longer apnea duration.

claim: At ~2 weeks of age, Scn1aΔE26 mice show a reduced ventilatory response to CO2.
source: At this same developmental time point, Scn1aΔE26 mice hypoventilate, exhibit frequent apneas under baseline conditions, and show a reduced ventilatory response to CO2.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing diminished minute ventilation response to CO2.

claim: The respiratory phenotype in Scn1aΔE26 mice is similar to what has been described in DS patients.
source: This respiratory phenotype is similar to what has been described DS patients (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to clinical observations supported by citation.

claim: Brainstem inhibitory neurons in the RTN of slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice show less spontaneous activity.
source: At the cellular level in a key brainstem respiratory chemoreceptor region known as the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), we found that inhibitory neurons expressing the A1783V pathological variant show less spontaneous activity
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings showing reduced basal firing rate.

claim: Brainstem inhibitory neurons in the RTN of slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice show a diminished ability to maintain firing during sustained depolarization.
source: At the cellular level in a key brainstem respiratory chemoreceptor region known as the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), we found that inhibitory neurons expressing the A1783V pathological variant show less spontaneous activity and a diminished ability to maintain firing during sustained depolarization.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings showing reduced action potential generation during current steps.

claim: The A1783V channel mutant disrupts channel expression or function by increasing voltage dependent inactivation.
source: This is consistent with the possibility that the A1783V channel mutant disrupts channel expression or function by increasing voltage dependent inactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from action potential kinetics data showing reduced depolarization rate and amplitude.

claim: Basal activity of excitatory chemosensitive RTN neurons was enhanced in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: Also consistent with a brainstem disinhibition mechanism, we found that basal activity and CO2/H+-sensitivity of excitatory chemosensitive RTN neurons was enhanced in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings showing higher baseline firing rate.

claim: CO2/H+-sensitivity of excitatory chemosensitive RTN neurons was enhanced in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: Also consistent with a brainstem disinhibition mechanism, we found that basal activity and CO2/H+-sensitivity of excitatory chemosensitive RTN neurons was enhanced in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings showing enhanced firing response to CO2.

claim: RTN chemoreceptor function is altered in the Scn1aΔE26 DS model.
source: Thus, our findings indicate that RTN chemoreceptors are a potential substrate for respiratory dysfunction in DS.
evidence: This is inferred from the cellular electrophysiology data showing altered activity of RTN neurons.

claim: RTN chemoreceptors may contribute to premature death in DS.
source: These results show that RTN chemoreceptor function is altered in this DS model and may contribute to premature death.
evidence: This is speculated based on the correlation between altered RTN function and premature death.

claim: Transcript containing the A1783V variant is expressed in brainstem tissue from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: Importantly, we also were able to detect the alanine to valine single nucleotide substitution at position 1772 (analogous to position 1783 in human) in 8 of 20 (40%) samples of Scn1aΔE26 tissue (Figure 1Aiii), indicating this missense mutation is expressed at the mRNA level.
evidence: This is supported by PCR amplification and sequencing data shown in Figure 1Aiii.

claim: Only wild type sequence was detected in Slc32a1cre/+ and Scn1afl/+ control tissue.
source: As expected, only wild type sequence was detected in Slc32a1cre/+ and Scn1afl/+ control tissue (Figure 1Aiii), suggesting there is minimal leaky expression of A1783V in the absence of Cre.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1Aiii.

claim: There is minimal leaky expression of A1783V in the absence of Cre.
source: As expected, only wild type sequence was detected in Slc32a1cre/+ and Scn1afl/+ control tissue (Figure 1Aiii), suggesting there is minimal leaky expression of A1783V in the absence of Cre.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of A1783V sequence in control tissue.

claim: Inhibitory Vgat+ cells are present in the RTN region and are in close proximity to excitatory Vglut2+ neurons.
source: Inhibitory Vgat+ cells were present in the RTN region and were in close proximity to excitatory Vglut2+ neurons (i.e., putative RTN chemoreceptors).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data.

claim: Both genotypes showed similar relative distributions of Vgat+ cells.
source: Both genotypes showed similar relative distributions of Vgat+ cells (T172 = 0.142, p=0.88).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of FISH data.

claim: Scn1a transcript is highly expressed in Vgat+ cells in slices from control mice.
source: We also observed numerous bright fluorescent puncta, which corresponded to Scn1a transcript in the soma of Vgat+ cells and, to a lesser extent, in Vglut2+ cells in slices from control mice (F3,321 = 24.07, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data.

claim: Scn1a transcript is expressed to a lesser extent in Vglut2+ cells in slices from control mice.
source: We also observed numerous bright fluorescent puncta, which corresponded to Scn1a transcript in the soma of Vgat+ cells and, to a lesser extent, in Vglut2+ cells in slices from control mice (F3,321 = 24.07, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data.

claim: In slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice, there is a modest reduction in Scn1a transcript in Vgat+ but not Vglut2+ cells.
source: In slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice, we found a modest reduction in Scn1a transcript in Vgat+ but not Vglut2+ cells (F3,321 = 24.07, p<0.05; see Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of FISH data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The A1783V pathogenic variant is expressed by brainstem inhibitory neurons.
source: Together with our sequencing data (Figure 1Aiii), these results suggest that the A1783V pathogenic variant is expressed by brainstem inhibitory neurons but possibly at slightly reduced levels compared to control.
evidence: This is inferred from sequencing and FISH data.

claim: The A1783V pathogenic variant is possibly expressed at slightly reduced levels compared to control.
source: Together with our sequencing data (Figure 1Aiii), these results suggest that the A1783V pathogenic variant is expressed by brainstem inhibitory neurons but possibly at slightly reduced levels compared to control.
evidence: This is inferred from the modest reduction in Scn1a transcript in Vgat+ cells.

claim: Cellular and behavioral phenotypes associated with Scn1aΔE26 mice may involve either reduced expression, impaired channel function, or both.
source: Therefore, cellular and behavioral phenotypes associated with Scn1aΔE26 mice (see below) may involve either reduced expression, impaired channel function, or both.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed reduction in transcript and predicted functional effects of the mutation.

claim: All TdT+ cells expressed Vgat, but not Vglut2, mRNA.
source: In a separate experiment to validate cell-type-specific Cre expression, we confirmed that all TdT+ cells expressed Vgat, but not Vglut2, mRNA (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation of Cre specificity.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice were born in the expected ratios.
source: Scn1aΔE26 mice were born in the expected ratios, were viable
evidence: This is an observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice were viable.
source: Scn1aΔE26 mice were born in the expected ratios, were viable
evidence: This is an observation from breeding experiments.

claim: By ~15 days postnatal, Scn1aΔE26 mice were similar in terms of body weight as their Slc32a1cre/+ control littermates.
source: and by ~15 days postnatal, were similar in terms of body weight (T46 = 1.62, p=0.11) and temperature (T26 = 0.77, p=0.44) as their Slc32a1cre/+ control littermates (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: By ~15 days postnatal, Scn1aΔE26 mice were similar in terms of temperature as their Slc32a1cre/+ control littermates.
source: and by ~15 days postnatal, were similar in terms of body weight (T46 = 1.62, p=0.11) and temperature (T26 = 0.77, p=0.44) as their Slc32a1cre/+ control littermates (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 pups show seizure-like behavior by ~2 weeks of age.
source: However, Scn1aΔE26 pups show seizure-like behavior by ~2 weeks of age (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations summarized in Table 1.

claim: Only 22.7% of Slc32a1cre/+ control mice showed seizure-like behavior, which mainly manifested as head-bobbing (category 1).
source: More specifically, based on the Racine seizure-behavior scoring paradigm, only 22.7% of Slc32a1cre/+ control mice (N = 22) showed seizure-like behavior, which mainly manifested as head-bobbing (category 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral scoring data in Table 1.

claim: 77.3% of Scn1aΔE26 mice showed severe seizure behavior.
source: By contrast, 77.3% of Scn1aΔE26 mice (N = 22) showed severe seizure behavior, including forelimb tremor (category 3), rearing alone (category 4) or in conjunction with falling over, and full-body tonic-clonic seizure (category 5).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral scoring data in Table 1.

claim: Several Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibited behavioral arrest that may reflect absence seizure-like activity.
source: Unlike Slc32a1cre/+control animals, several of the mutant mice exhibited behavioral arrest that may reflect absence seizure-like activity.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral monitoring with speculative interpretation.

claim: All Scn1aΔE26 mice (N = 9) developed tonic-clonic seizures when core body temperature was increased from 37°C to 42.5°C.
source: When core body temperature was increased from 37°C to 42.5°C (0.5°C increments every 2 min) all Scn1aΔE26 mice (N = 9) developed tonic-clonic seizures (category 5) at an average body temperature of 41.1 ± 0.2°C (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by thermal seizure induction experiments summarized in Table 2.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice developed tonic-clonic seizures at an average body temperature of 41.1 ± 0.2°C.
source: When core body temperature was increased from 37°C to 42.5°C (0.5°C increments every 2 min) all Scn1aΔE26 mice (N = 9) developed tonic-clonic seizures (category 5) at an average body temperature of 41.1 ± 0.2°C (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by thermal seizure induction experiments summarized in Table 2.

claim: None of the Slc32a1cre/+ litter mate controls (N = 10) showed seizure activity up to the cut-off temperature of 42.5°C.
source: Conversely, none of the Slc32a1cre/+- litter mate controls (N = 10) showed seizure activity up to the cut-off temperature of 42.5°C (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by thermal seizure induction experiments summarized in Table 2.

claim: Heterozygous Scn1a knockout mice do not develop temperature-induced seizures until ~18 days of age.
source: These results differ somewhat from previous work that showed heterozygous Scn1a knockout mice do not develop temperature-induced seizures until ~18 days of age (Oakley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature supported by citation.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice begin to die at ~12 days of age, reaching 100% lethality by 23 days postnatal.
source: In addition to increased febrile seizure propensity, Scn1aΔE26 also begin to die at ~12 days of age, reaching 100% lethality by 23 days postnatal (Figure 1F and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Early onset of premature death in Scn1aΔE26 mice occurs ~1 week prior to mortality in heterozygous Scn1a knockout mice on a pure C57BL/6J background.
source: This early onset of premature death in Scn1aΔE26 mice occurs ~1 week prior to mortality in heterozygous Scn1a knockout mice on a pure C57BL/6J background (Yu et al., 2006; Catterall, 2012)
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature supported by citations.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice (90% C57BL/6J background) have a particularly severe phenotype.
source: This early onset of premature death in Scn1aΔE26 mice occurs ~1 week prior to mortality in heterozygous Scn1a knockout mice on a pure C57BL/6J background (Yu et al., 2006; Catterall, 2012), suggesting Scn1aΔE26 mice (90% C57BL/6J background) have a particularly severe phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of mortality timing between different mouse models.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice showed large amplitude polyspike activity that lasted for an average duration of 15.6 ± 0.8 s.
source: Consistent with frequent polyspike activity observed in the ECoG recordings of DS patients (Bender et al., 2012), Scn1aΔE26 mice showed large amplitude (at least twice baseline) polyspike activity that lasted for an average duration of 15.6 ± 0.8 s (Figure 2A–Bi).
evidence: This is supported by ECoG recording data shown in Figure 2A-Bi.

claim: Polyspike events in Scn1aΔE26 mice always occurred in conjunction with seizure activity (category 4–5).
source: These events always occurred in conjunction with seizure activity (category 4–5) but were frequently preceded by brief behavioral arrest.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous video and ECoG recordings.

claim: Polyspike events in Scn1aΔE26 mice were frequently preceded by brief behavioral arrest.
source: These events always occurred in conjunction with seizure activity (category 4–5) but were frequently preceded by brief behavioral arrest.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous video and ECoG recordings.

claim: The duration of polyspike events in Scn1aΔE26 mice were considerably shorter than spike wave discharges associated with absence epilepsy that typically last for >1 s.
source: The duration of these polyspike events were considerably shorter than spike wave discharges associated with absence epilepsy that typically last for >1 s (Letts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to established characteristics of absence epilepsy supported by citation.

claim: Slc32a1cre/+ littermate control animals showed minimal large amplitude spike activity.
source: Conversely, Slc32a1cre/+ littermate control animals showed minimal large amplitude spike activity; any detectable events were of a short duration 7.55 ± 0.6 s (Figure 2A–Bi)
evidence: This is supported by ECoG recording data shown in Figure 2A-Bi.

claim: Detectable spike events in Slc32a1cre/+ control animals were of a short duration 7.55 ± 0.6 s.
source: Conversely, Slc32a1cre/+ littermate control animals showed minimal large amplitude spike activity; any detectable events were of a short duration 7.55 ± 0.6 s (Figure 2A–Bi)
evidence: This is supported by ECoG recording data shown in Figure 2A-Bi.

claim: Detectable spike events in Slc32a1cre/+ control animals occurred when the animal was exhibiting exploratory behavior and less obvious seizure like activity (category 0–2) or freezing behavior.
source: and occurred when the animal was exhibiting exploratory behavior and less obvious seizure like activity (category 0–2) or freezing behavior.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous video and ECoG recordings.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice show epileptic spike activity with a frequency of 9.167 ± 3.9 events/2 hr.
source: Based on this criteria, Scn1aΔE26 and Slc32a1cre/+ control mice show epileptic spike activity with a frequency 9.167 ± 3.9 events/2 hr and of 0.25 ± 0.1 events/2 hr, respectively (T5 = 2.28, p<0.05) (Figure 2Bii).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of ECoG recordings shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: Slc32a1cre/+ control mice show epileptic spike activity with a frequency of 0.25 ± 0.1 events/2 hr.
source: Based on this criteria, Scn1aΔE26 and Slc32a1cre/+ control mice show epileptic spike activity with a frequency 9.167 ± 3.9 events/2 hr and of 0.25 ± 0.1 events/2 hr, respectively (T5 = 2.28, p<0.05) (Figure 2Bii).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of ECoG recordings shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: Epileptic events in Scn1aΔE26 mice were composed of high alpha and beta frequencies.
source: Power spectral analysis of poly-spike events in Slc32a1cre/+ and epileptic events in Scn1aΔE26 mice show that epileptic events were composed of high alpha and beta frequencies (F4, 840 = 5.605, p<0.001) (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by power spectral analysis shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice are phenotypically similar to global and inhibitory neuron-specific Scn1a haploinsufficient models of DS.
source: These results suggest Scn1aΔE26 mice are phenotypically similar to global and inhibitory neuron-specific Scn1a haploinsufficient models of DS (Yu et al., 2006; Kalume et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2018)
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of phenotypes with previous models supported by citations.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice have an accelerated time course for manifestation of pathological features including spontaneous and heat-induced seizures as well as premature death.
source: These results suggest Scn1aΔE26 mice are phenotypically similar to global and inhibitory neuron-specific Scn1a haploinsufficient models of DS (Yu et al., 2006; Kalume et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2018), but with an accelerated time course for manifestation of pathological features including spontaneous and heat-induced seizures as well as premature death.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of timing of phenotype onset with previous models.

claim: DS patients showed peri-ictal breathing problems including hypoventilation and apnea prior to the manifestation of bradycardia.
source: For example, DS patients showed peri-ictal breathing problems including hypoventilation and apnea prior to the manifestation of bradycardia, a slower than normal heart rate (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: Patients with DS exhibited a blunted ventilatory response to CO2.
source: Patients with DS also exhibited a blunted ventilatory response to CO2 (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: Respiratory dysfunction, possibly at the level of respiratory chemoreceptors, contributes to the pathology of DS.
source: This finding suggests that respiratory dysfunction, possibly at the level of respiratory chemoreceptors (neurons that regulate breathing in response to changes in tissue CO2/H+), contributes to the pathology of DS.
evidence: This is speculated based on clinical observations of blunted CO2 response.

claim: There is evidence that activity of serotonergic neurons in the dorsal and medullary raphe regions in rats are suppressed during ictal and post-ictal periods.
source: Consistent with the latter possibility, there is evidence that activity of serotonergic neurons in the dorsal and medullary raphe regions in rats are suppressed during ictal and post-ictal periods (Zhan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Serotonin is a potent modulator of breathing and arousal.
source: Serotonin is a potent modulator of breathing and arousal (Richerson, 2004; Buchanan and Richerson, 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of serotonergic drive during seizures may contribute to SUDEP.
source: therefore, it is possible that loss of this drive during seizures contributes to SUDEP.
evidence: This is speculated based on the role of serotonin in breathing and arousal.

claim: Pharmacological augmentation of serotonergic signaling can prevent seizure-induced respiratory arrest in a mouse model of epilepsy.
source: This possibility is supported by evidence that pharmacological augmentation of serotonergic signaling can prevent seizure-induced respiratory arrest in a mouse model of epilepsy and may improve seizure control in DS patients (Tupal and Faingold, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Pharmacological augmentation of serotonergic signaling may improve seizure control in DS patients.
source: This possibility is supported by evidence that pharmacological augmentation of serotonergic signaling can prevent seizure-induced respiratory arrest in a mouse model of epilepsy and may improve seizure control in DS patients (Tupal and Faingold, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Some epilepsy patients show breathing abnormalities under baseline inter-ictal conditions including a reduced ventilatory response to CO2.
source: However, some epilepsy patients show breathing abnormalities under baseline inter-ictal conditions including a reduced ventilatory response to CO2 (i.e., chemoreflex) (Sainju et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: Epilepsy-associated mutations may directly affect brainstem respiratory centers to compromise breathing under inter-ictal conditions.
source: Based on this, we consider a yet unexplored possibility that epilepsy-associated mutations may directly affect brainstem respiratory centers to compromise breathing under inter-ictal conditions, and thus serve as a common substrate for both seizures and respiratory dysfunction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on clinical observations.

claim: Epilepsy-associated mutations may serve as a common substrate for both seizures and respiratory dysfunction.
source: Based on this, we consider a yet unexplored possibility that epilepsy-associated mutations may directly affect brainstem respiratory centers to compromise breathing under inter-ictal conditions, and thus serve as a common substrate for both seizures and respiratory dysfunction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Compared to control animals, Scn1aΔE26 mice show diminished respiratory output under room air conditions.
source: We found that compared to control animals, Scn1aΔE26 mice show diminished respiratory output under room air conditions.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data showing reduced frequency, tidal volume, and minute ventilation.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibit suppressed respiratory frequency (211 ± 16 bpm) compared to control (256 ± 11 bpm).
source: Specifically, Scn1aΔE26 exhibit suppressed frequency (256 ± 11 bpm for control compared to 211 ± 16 bpm for Scn1aΔE26; T33 = 2.43; p<0.05)
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibit suppressed tidal volume (8.9 ± 1.9 μl/g) compared to control (14.8 ± 2.0 μl/g).
source: tidal volume (14.8 ± 2.0 μl/g for control compared to 8.9 ± 1.9 μl/g for Scn1aΔE26, T33 = 2.02, p<0.05)
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibit suppressed minute ventilation (2.7 ± 0.5 μl/min/g) compared to control (3.6 ± 0.5 μl/min/g).
source: and minute ventilation (3.6 ± 0.5 μl/min/g for control compared to 2.7 ± 0.5 μl/min/g for Scn1aΔE26; T33 = 2.01, p<0.05; Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Both control and Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibit apneic events at similar frequencies.
source: Although both control and Scn1aΔE26 mice exhibit apneic events at similar frequencies (0.23 ± 0.1/min for control and 0.11 ± 0.04/min for Scn1aΔE26; p=0.6)
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: The duration of apneic events were longer in Scn1aΔE26 mice (1,350 ± 99.2 ms) compared to controls (1,104 ± 58.6 ms).
source: the duration of these events were longer in Scn1aΔE26 mice (Figure 3E; 1,104 ± 58.6 ms for controls versus 1,350 ± 99.2 ms Scn1aΔE26; T51 = 2.135; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 mice had a diminished capacity to increase respiratory frequency in response to graded increases in CO2.
source: We also found that Scn1aΔE26 mice had a diminished capacity to increase respiratory frequency in response to graded increases in CO2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Respiratory frequency in 7% CO2 was higher in controls (363.1 ± 7.7 bpm) versus Scn1aΔE26 (300.7 ± 17.4 bpm).
source: Specifically, respiratory frequency in 7% CO2 (balance O2) was higher in controls (363.1 ± 7.7 bpm; N = 22) versus Scn1aΔE26 (300.7 ± 17.4 bpm; N = 17; F1,37 = 5.69, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: Tidal volume responses to CO2/H+ are similar between genotypes.
source: Although tidal volume responses to CO2/H+ are similar between genotypes (p=0.47)
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: Total respiratory output, as measured by minute ventilation, was diminished in Scn1aΔE26 mice compared to controls.
source: total respiratory output, as measured by minute ventilation— the product of respiratory frequency and tidal volume—was diminished in Scn1aΔE26 mice compared to controls (F3,111 = 3.167, p<0.05; Figure 3G–H and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Increasing inspired CO2 from 0% to 3% increased minute ventilation in control mice by 3.3 ± 0.5 μl/min/g.
source: Specifically, increasing inspired CO2 from 0% to 3% increased minute ventilation in control mice by 3.3 ± 0.5 μl/min/g (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: Increasing inspired CO2 from 0% to 3% led to a much smaller and non-significant increase in minute ventilation among Scn1aΔE26 mice (increase of 1.5 ± 0.5 μl/min/g).
source: These same conditions, however, led to a much smaller and non-significant increase in minute ventilation among Scn1aΔE26 mice (increase of 1.5 ± 0.5 μl/min/g; p=0.07).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography measurements.

claim: Inhibitory neurons from Scn1aΔE26 mice have lower basal activity (9.902 ± 0.64 Hz) than those of Slc32a1cre/+ control mice (14.39 ± 1.5 Hz).
source: For example, whole-cell current-clamp recordings from inhibitory neurons in the RTN region in slices from Slc32a1cre/+ or Scn1aΔE26 mice show that inhibitory neurons from Scn1aΔE26 mice have lower basal activity than those of Slc32a1cre/+ control mice (14.39 ± 1.5 Hz for Slc32a1cre/+ vs. 9.902 ± 0.64 Hz for Scn1aΔE26; T60 = 2.97, p<0.01; Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 inhibitory neurons fired fewer action potentials in response to depolarizing current steps (0–300 pA; Δ 20 pA) from a holding potential of −80 mV.
source: Furthermore, Scn1aΔE26 inhibitory neurons fired fewer action potentials in response to depolarizing current steps (0–300 pA; Δ 20 pA) from a holding potential of −80 mV.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings.

claim: Scn1aΔE26 inhibitory neurons showed pronounced spike amplitude and frequency decrement during large (200–300 pA) sustained (1,000 ms) current injections.
source: This activity deficit became more pronounced during large (200–300 pA) sustained (1,000 ms) current injections where inhibitory neurons from Scn1aΔE26 mice showed pronounced spike amplitude and frequency decrement (Figure 4A,D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4A,D.

claim: The number of spikes elicited by a + 300 pA current step (1,000 ms) was 53.7 ± 11 for Slc32a1cre/+ controls compared to 13.9 ± 6.4 for Scn1aΔE26.
source: That is, the number of spikes elicited by a + 300 pA current step (1,000 ms) was 53.7 ± 11 for Slc32a1cre/+ controls (N = 13) compared to 13.9 ± 6.4 for Scn1aΔE26 (N = 20; F15,465 = 9.536; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings.

claim: Inhibitory neurons from each genotype had similar input resistance.
source: We also found that inhibitory neurons from each genotype had similar input resistance (517.6 ± 82.2 MΩ for Slc32a1cre/+ control vs. 519.2 ± 38.9 MΩ for Scn1aΔE26; T25 = 0.02; p=0.3; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The A1783V pathological variant is located in the S6 segment of domain 4.
source: The A1783V pathological variant is located in the S6 segment of domain 4 (Marini et al., 2007; Lossin, 2009)
evidence: This is established structural information supported by citations.

claim: The S6 segment of domain 4 is a region thought to regulate voltage-dependent inactivation.
source: The A1783V pathological variant is located in the S6 segment of domain 4 (Marini et al., 2007; Lossin, 2009), a region thought to regulate voltage-dependent inactivation (Catterall, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about channel structure-function supported by citation.

claim: The Scn1a A1783V variant results in loss of function, in part, by causing Nav1.1 channels to inactivate at more negative voltages.
source: Based on our evidence that A1783V is expressed in tissue form Scn1aΔE26 mice (Figure 1Aiii) and since inhibitory neurons from these animals show reduced excitability (Figure 4A–B), we hypothesized that the Scn1a A1783V variant results in loss of function, in part, by causing Nav1.1 channels to inactivate at more negative voltages.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the location of the mutation and observed electrophysiological phenotype.

claim: Spontaneous action potentials in inhibitory neurons in slices of Slc32a1cre/+ control mice showed a higher amplitude (73.5 ± 1.9 mV) than Scn1aΔE26 (61.9 ± 2.6 mV).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, when examining spontaneous action potentials (as measured under resting conditions with a 0 pA holding current) in inhibitory neurons in slices of Scn1aΔE26 and Slc32a1cre/+ control mice, the latter showed a higher amplitude (73.5 ± 1.9 mV) than Scn1aΔE26 (61.9 ± 2.6 mV; F1,95 = 9.931, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings.

claim: The maximum rate of depolarization was higher for Slc32a1cre/+ controls (134.4 ± 5.0 mV/mS) compared to Scn1aΔE26 (89.4 ± 5.3 mV/mS).
source: The maximum rate of depolarization was higher for Slc32a1cre/+ controls (134.4 ± 5.0 mV/mS) compared to Scn1aΔE26 (89.4 ± 5.3 mV/mS; F1,96 = 35.2, p<0.0001; see Figure 5A,D–F and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5A,D-F.

claim: Action potential threshold was higher in inhibitory neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 (−29.2 ± 0.9 mV) compared to Slc32a1cre/+ controls (−32.4 ± 0.6 mV).
source: Action potential threshold was also higher in inhibitory neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 (−29.2 ± 0.9 mV) compared to Slc32a1cre/+ controls (−32.4 ± 0.6 mV; F1,95 = 7.403, p<0.05; Figure 5A,F).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5A,F.

claim: Differences in action potential waveform properties between genotypes were minimized when cells are held at a negative voltage to remove Na+ channel inactivation.
source: We found that differences in action potential waveform properties between genotypes were minimized when cells are held at a negative voltage to remove Na+ channel inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings with different pre-potentials.

claim: Holding inhibitory neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice at a negative pre-potential by injecting a hyperpolarizing current (−100 pA; 1,000 ms) increased action potential amplitude to 78.01 ± 2.0 mV.
source: For example, holding inhibitory neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice at a negative pre-potential by injecting a hyperpolarizing current (−100 pA; 1,000 ms) increased action potential amplitude (78.01 ± 2.0 mV; F1, 95 = 9.931, p<0.0001) to an amount similar to spikes from Slc32a1cre/+ control cells (81.05 ± 1.2 mV; p=0.83) (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5B,E.

claim: Under negative pre-potential conditions, the maximum rate of depolarization increased to 140.3 ± 5.441 mV/ms in Scn1aΔE26 inhibitory neurons.
source: Under these conditions, the maximum rate of depolarization also increased 140.3 ± 5.441 mV/ms (F 1, 96 = 35.21, p<0.0001) (Figure 5B,D and Figure 5—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: The maximum rate of depolarization after negative pre-potential in Scn1aΔE26 neurons was similar to that measured in spontaneous spikes from Slc32a1cre/+ control animals.
source: this rate was similar to that measured in spontaneous spikes from Slc32a1cre/+ control animals (p>0.99)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of electrophysiology data.

claim: The maximum rate of depolarization after negative pre-potential in Scn1aΔE26 neurons was slower than spikes from Slc32a1cre/+ control cells following a negative pre-potential (166.6 ± 7.3 mV/mS).
source: but slower than spikes from Slc32a1cre/+ control cells following a negative pre-potential (166.6 ± 7.3 mV/mS, F1,96 = 35.21, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of electrophysiology data.

claim: Holding inhibitory neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice at a negative pre-potential lowered the threshold for spike initiation to −35.68 ± 0.7 mV.
source: Holding inhibitory neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice at a negative pre-potential also lowered the threshold for spike initiation (−35.68 ± 0.7 mV; F1, 95 = 7.403, p<0.001) to a level similar to Slc32a1cre/+ control cells (−37.2 ± 1.2 mV; F1, 95 = 7.403, p=0.06) (Figure 5B,F).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5B,F.

claim: Loss of Scn1a function involves enhanced Nav1.1 inactivation.
source: Although it is possible that diminished expression of channel containing A1783V (Figure 1C) may also contribute to this electrophysiological phenotype; since transcript containing A1783V appears to be abundantly expressed (Figure 1Aiii), we speculate that loss of Scn1a function involves enhanced Nav1.1 inactivation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the electrophysiological data and expression data.

claim: Loss of inhibitory tone by expression of Scn1a A1783V would enhance basal activity and CO2/H+ sensitivity of glutamatergic chemosensitive neurons.
source: Based on previous evidence suggests inhibitory neurons in the RTN region can regulate activity of chemosensitive neurons (Ott et al., 2011), we predict that loss of inhibitory tone by expression of Scn1a A1783V would enhance basal activity and CO2/H+ sensitivity of glutamatergic chemosensitive neurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on previous literature and the observed reduction in inhibitory neuron activity.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons in slices from Slc32a1cre/+ control mice had an average basal activity of 1.3 ± 0.4 Hz under control conditions (5% CO2; pH 7.3).
source: Chemosensitive RTN neurons in slices from Slc32a1cre/+ control mice had an average basal activity of 1.3 ± 0.4 Hz under control conditions (5% CO2; pH 7.3).
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons in control slices were strongly inhibited by decreasing CO2 to 3% (pHo = 7.6) (1.02 ± 0.3 Hz).
source: These cells were strongly inhibited by decreasing CO2 to 3% (pHo = 7.6) (1.02 ± 0.3 Hz)
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons in control slices showed a linear firing increase in response to 7% CO2 (pHo = 7.2) (2.4 ± 0.5 Hz) and 10% CO2 (pHo = 7.0) (2.8 ± 0.4 Hz).
source: and showed a linear firing increase in response to 7% (pHo = 7.2) (2.4 ± 0.5 Hz) and 10% CO2 (pHo = 7.0) (2.8 ± 0.4 Hz) (Figure 6A,B–C).
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 6A,B-C.

claim: The CO2 response profile of control RTN neurons is consistent with type I chemoreceptors (pH50 = 7.3).
source: This CO2 response profile is consistent with type I chemoreceptors (pH50 = 7.3), which were described previously in a Phox2b mouse reporter line (Lazarenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously characterized chemoreceptor types supported by citation.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice were more active under control conditions (5% CO2) (2.4 ± 0.35 Hz).
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, chemosensitive RTN neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice were more active under control conditions (5% CO2) (2.4 ± 0.35 Hz) (Figure 6C) (T21 = 2.223, p<0.05)
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice showed an enhanced firing response to high CO2/H+ (slope: 0.37 ± 0.01) compared to control (slope: 0.3 ± 0.01).
source: and showed an enhanced firing response to high CO2/H+ (Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 1) (slope: 0.3 ± 0.01 Slc32a1cre/+ vs. 0.37 ± 0.01 Scn1aΔE26, F1,4 = 8.04, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All CO2/H+-sensitive neurons included in the study were phox2b-positive.
source: We confirmed that all CO2/H+-sensitive neurons (Slc32a1cre/+ control n = 12; Scn1aΔE26 n = 11) included in this study were phox2b-positive.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical confirmation.

claim: Loss of Scn1a from inhibitory neurons in the forebrain, but not the brainstem, resulted in premature death.
source: Although mechanisms contributing to respiratory dysfunction in DS are unknown, previous work showed that loss of Scn1a from inhibitory neurons in the forebrain, but not the brainstem where respiratory control centers are located, resulted in premature death (Cheah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Respiratory dysfunction in DS is a secondary consequence of cortical seizure activity propagating to and disrupting brainstem function.
source: These results suggest respiratory dysfunction in DS is a secondary consequence of cortical seizure activity propagating to and disrupting brainstem function.
evidence: This is inferred from previous findings about the role of forebrain Scn1a deletion.

claim: Apnea and arterial oxygen desaturation occurred when cortical seizure activity spread to the amygdala.
source: For example, recent work in humans showed that apnea and arterial oxygen desaturation occurred when cortical seizure activity spread to the amygdala (Dlouhy et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: SUDEP can occur in epilepsy patients in the absence of an overt seizure or outside the peri-ictal period.
source: However, SUDEP can also occur in epilepsy patients in the absence of an overt seizure or outside the peri-ictal period (Lhatoo and Shorvon, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Patients with temporal lobe epilepsy show widespread alterations in neural network activity including at the level of the brainstem.
source: Consistent with this possibility, patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (a common type of focal epilepsy) show widespread alterations in neural network activity including at the level of the brainstem (Englot et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: The frequency response elicited by photo-activation of RTN chemoreceptors in vitro was eliminated by systemically blocking inhibition with picrotoxin and strychnine.
source: For example, the frequency response elicited by photo-activation of RTN chemoreceptors in vitro was eliminated by systemically blocking inhibition with picrotoxin and strychnine (Cregg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Other respiratory elements also contribute to the observed hypoventilation phenotype in Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: Therefore, although RTN chemoreceptor function is perturbed in Scn1aΔE26 mice, it is likely that other respiratory elements also contribute to the observed hypoventilation phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the complexity of respiratory control and the dependence on inhibitory neurotransmission.

claim: Loss of inhibitory tone within the pre-bötzinger complex has been shown to decrease respiratory frequency.
source: This is notable because loss of inhibitory tone within this region has been shown to decrease respiratory frequency (Del Negro et al., 2018; Baertsch et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The breathing phenotype in Scn1aΔE26 mice under high CO2 conditions preferentially involves diminished respiratory frequency but otherwise normal tidal volume.
source: and the breathing phenotype in Scn1aΔE26 mice under high CO2 conditions preferentially involves diminished respiratory frequency but otherwise normal tidal volume (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmography data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Scn1a missense mutations represent ~40% of DS-associated mutations.
source: Despite the prevalence of Scn1a missense mutations in DS (Parihar and Ganesh, 2013), few studies have characterized the pathophysiology associated with specific mutant alleles.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The aberrant products of Scn1a missense mutations are potentially expressed, thus representing a novel therapeutic target that is absent from haploinsufficient models of DS.
source: This is particularly important for the development of patient-directed therapies because the aberrant products of Scn1a missense mutations are potentially expressed, thus representing a novel therapeutic target that is absent from haploinsufficient models of DS.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between missense mutations and haploinsufficiency.

claim: Expression of the Scn1a pathological variant A1783V in inhibitory neurons results in seizures and premature death on an accelerated time scale compared to haploinsufficient DS models.
source: Here, we show that expression of the Scn1a pathological variant A1783V in inhibitory neurons results in seizures and premature death on an accelerated time scale compared to haploinsufficient DS models (Catterall, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival and seizure onset data with previous models.

claim: The repetitive firing characteristics of inhibitory neurons from Scn1aΔE26 mice is consistent with loss of function due to increased Nav1.1 channel inactivation.
source: Inhibitory neurons from Scn1aΔE26 mice showed a modest reduction in channel transcript (Figure 1C) that may contribute to loss of inhibitory tone (Figures 4–5); however, transcript containing the A1783V variant was expressed in tissue from Scn1aΔE26 mice (Figure 1A) and the repetitive firing characteristics of inhibitory neurons from Scn1aΔE26 mice is consistent with loss of function due to increased Nav1.1 channel inactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data showing effects of pre-potentials on action potential properties.

claim: An effective treatment for Scn1a A1783V-associated pathology might be to selectively potentiate Nav1.1 channel activity by slowing voltage-dependent inactivation.
source: Therefore, an effective treatment for Scn1a A1783V-associated pathology might be to selectively potentiate Nav1.1 channel activity by slowing voltage-dependent inactivation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the proposed mechanism of loss of function.

claim: Expression of Scn1a A1783V in inhibitory neurons results in clinical features of DS including spontaneous seizures and respiratory dysfunction.
source: In sum, our results show that expression of Scn1a A1783V in inhibitory neurons results in clinical features of DS including spontaneous seizures and respiratory dysfunction.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by experimental data.

claim: Brainstem inhibitory neurons in the RTN of slices from Scn1aΔE26 are less excitable.
source: At the cellular level, brainstem inhibitory neurons in the RTN of slices from Scn1aΔE26 are less excitable
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current-clamp recordings.

claim: Glutamatergic chemosensitive neurons in the RTN are more excitable in slices from Scn1aΔE26 mice.
source: whereas glutamatergic chemosensitive neurons are more excitable.
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recordings.

claim: RTN chemoreceptors are a potential substrate for respiratory dysfunction in DS.
source: Thus, our findings indicate that RTN chemoreceptors are a potential substrate for respiratory dysfunction in DS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed alterations in RTN chemoreceptor function.
